# Check a Player-Value Model With Expected-Direction Tests When No Ground Truth Exists

**What it is** — Paul Sabin offers three plots "to validate some of our assumptions and some of our results" (oZsFyPGij0U [17:30], [18:03]).
1. **Separation check.** Quarterback value against average offensive-line value: correlated, "not as strong as you would think," with teams that have strong lines and weak quarterbacks and the reverse (oZsFyPGij0U [18:03], [18:34]).
2. **Within-unit check.** The two linemen with the most snaps: correlated but "not perfectly," so credit can be split between them (oZsFyPGij0U [18:34]).
3. **Direction-of-change check.** Value at the new team against the old team for players who moved. College transfers fall above the one-to-one line (better at the new school); NFL movers fall below it (typically a bit worse, which he links to players nearing 30 whose teams let them go) (oZsFyPGij0U [19:05], [19:35]).
The slopes and correlations are shown only as plots; no numbers are given in the transcript. He also treats a backup center doing worse than the starter as support for the center result (oZsFyPGij0U [21:39], [22:09]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is that these are outcomes "you would expect" if told in advance, so the model reproducing them is reassuring (oZsFyPGij0U [19:35]). Inference: these tests can only rule out a model that fails an obvious expectation; they do not show the values are accurate.

**When to apply** — When a new rating has no ground truth: write the expected direction of three or four checks before looking at output (does a unit's top player separate from its neighbors; do movers change in the direction age or context predicts). Eric's baseline: no direct link; the method baseline has no model-validation rule for player value.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested. The talk shows no out-of-sample or predictive test of player or position value, so these checks cannot support claims of accuracy; the summary's own limits section says the same. The transfer interpretation (age and who teams release) is the speaker's reading, with no data shown on age. Selection matters: players who change teams are not a random sample. Do not report these plots as validation to coaches.

**Example** — The speaker's own: NFL movers fall below the diagonal, which he reads as the expected decline for players after a first contract (oZsFyPGij0U [19:35]).

# Usage Bias: A Model Can Undervalue a Passer on a Run-Heavy Team, and a Pass Rusher Who Forces Runs

**What it is** — Paul Sabin names the main deficiency of his model: a quarterback who is very good at passing but whose coach does not use him that way (his example is Russell Wilson) may not show up as high as he should (oZsFyPGij0U [16:28]). He raises the mirror case on defense, Aaron Donald, typically considered the best defensive player. Against the pass his win rates are "so much better than everyone else it's not even on the chart," but against the run he is "not that great," and teams can usually run more effectively with him on the field (oZsFyPGij0U [16:28], [16:58]). Sabin's argument for Donald's value is that you would rather force a team to run, since running is less efficient (oZsFyPGij0U [16:58]). His planned fix is separate run and pass models next season, so players are not hurt by how they are used (oZsFyPGij0U [16:28], [16:58]). He also mentions Derrick Henry as roughly a top-10 impact player going into the playoffs (oZsFyPGij0U [15:58]). In recent NFL seasons the model's top players were Patrick Mahomes and Lamar Jackson, as spoken (oZsFyPGij0U [15:58]).

**Why it works** — Not a mechanism claim. The speaker's account is that a single value number pools run and pass plays, so a player whose strength lies on one side is graded on the play mix his coach chooses (oZsFyPGij0U [16:28]). The Donald point (forcing less efficient plays) is the speaker's assertion with no figures given.

**When to apply** — As a standing question when reading any single-number player grade: what is the player's usage, and what would the grade be if the coach called the plays differently? Inference: PFF-style grades and snap-based values at Baylor have the same exposure to play-calling mix. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: these are two named examples and a stated plan, with no numbers shown and no tested fix. The Donald claim about run-defense performance is a recollection ("teams usually can run more effectively when he's on the field"), not data in the talk. One case does not show how large the bias is across positions. The planned run and pass split was not built at the time of the talk, so no result exists.

**Example** — The speaker's own, above: Wilson (strong passer, run-heavy team) and Donald (elite pass rusher, weaker against the run) are the two illustrations of usage and play-type confounding.

**Related** — [[framework--position-variance-and-informative-priors-in-football-plus-minus]]; [[heuristic--separate-predictive-and-descriptive-versions-of-a-player-value-model]].

# Pricing a Protected Draft Pick as a Financial Option, in Basketball Units

**What it is** — Benjamin Foster (with co-author Michael Bins, caption spelling) prices a draft pick plus its protection scheme (a "draft pick asset") in player-value terms, not money (SIn6IyYQEVI [00:31], [01:02], [03:05]). A protection is a condition that lets the trading team keep the pick if it lands in a protected range, with the pick rolling over to later years (the Lakers 2015 pick was top-5 protected in 2015, top-3 for a couple of years, then unprotected in 2018) (SIn6IyYQEVI [02:02] to [03:05]). The analogy is a financial option: the protection plays the part of the contract terms, and the volatility of the underlying value matters (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:40], [08:10]). He does not use the option math directly, only its principles (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:10], [08:40]). Three steps (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:40]):
1. **Characterize volatility of the underlying asset.** Module one: an Elo-rating season simulation that gives a distribution of finishing position (1 means worst, to match how picks are dealt), run 10,000 times over the roughly 20 remaining games at the trade deadline (SIn6IyYQEVI [09:10], [09:40]). Module two: cumulative distributions of player value by pick position, using Basketball-Reference history for first-round picks, with win shares as the metric (SIn6IyYQEVI [10:11], [10:42]).
2. **Assess the contract conditions.** A 10,000-run Monte Carlo combines lottery probabilities and the protection scheme into a distribution of win shares summed over a player's first five years (SIn6IyYQEVI [11:14], [11:45]).
3. **Account for market risk** with a Wang transform (see [[heuristic--market-risk-preference-differs-by-pick-position-in-the-draft-pick-model]]), reducing the distribution to a single price (SIn6IyYQEVI [12:16], [13:17]).
He states the purpose is to help a team decide where to place protections when trading a pick away or trading for one (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:09]). Because millions of protection schemes exist, one base pick can have millions of trade values (SIn6IyYQEVI [04:07]). The model is modular, so the player value metric can be swapped (SIn6IyYQEVI [10:11], [19:23]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is the option parallel: how likely the pick is to fall inside versus outside the protected range drives value (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:40]). He gives no tested argument that this transfer from finance is accurate; he says they adapt the principles "with our own methods" (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:40]).

**When to apply** — As a template for any asset that arrives as an uncertain outcome with contract conditions: model the uncertainty source, apply the conditions in simulation, then price. Inference: for Baylor, the closest analogs are recruiting and portal classes (an uncertain future player value) rather than any monitoring work; the applications note flags low direct use for Applied Performance. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one worked example (see [[case-study--lakers-2015-pick-protections-removed-about-half-its-value]]), calibration from few pick-for-pick trades, and no outcome test. Limits the speaker names: the season simulation does not account for player movement, the work was done on personal computers with limited time, and time discounting and the option value of rolling a pick over are not explicitly modeled (SIn6IyYQEVI [14:48], [19:23], [22:26]). College rosters have no barter market with protections, so the option analogy may not carry over; the outcome data are NBA win shares for first-round picks only.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the Lakers 2015 first-round pick that went from the Suns to the Sixers at the 2015 deadline, priced with and without its top-5 protection (SIn6IyYQEVI [02:33], [12:46]).

**Related** — [[principle--value-an-uncertain-asset-by-its-outcome-distribution-not-its-mean]]; [[claim--traded-pick-protections-cluster-at-top-5-10-and-14]]; [[case-study--lakers-2015-pick-protections-removed-about-half-its-value]].

# Value an Uncertain Asset by Its Whole Outcome Distribution, Not Its Mean

**What it is** — Benjamin Foster shows that two assets with different tails can have similar averages. A base draft pick "looks like a distribution of possible pick position outcomes," so trading it gives the other team that set of outcomes (SIn6IyYQEVI [03:36]). A protection changes the distribution, not just its center (SIn6IyYQEVI [04:07]). Taking the mean "doesn't account for the variance," and the extreme outcomes (picks one through three, the chance of getting LeBron James or "someone who might change your franchise's history") are exactly what protection removes, so the model weights them (SIn6IyYQEVI [12:46], [13:17]). In the unprotected case the priced value sits far to the right of the mean because of the tail; in the protected case the price is "relatively close to the expected value" (SIn6IyYQEVI [15:49]). The tool is a risk adjustment (the Wang transform) with a market price of risk (SIn6IyYQEVI [13:17], [13:47]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reason is that teams care about outcomes in the tails, and the market prices that preference (SIn6IyYQEVI [13:17], [14:18]). He gives no empirical test that the adjustment is correct.

**When to apply** — When comparing options with different spreads (a high-ceiling prospect versus a safe contributor): show the range of outcomes in one unit, then say which end the decision values. Inference: a recruiting board could express each prospect as best, typical and worst case in one unit and compare classes by spread, as the applications note proposes. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the speaker presents a method and one worked example with no validation, and the risk parameter is calibrated on few pick-for-pick trades (SIn6IyYQEVI [14:48]). If decision makers value only the average, or the outcome data are too thin to build a distribution (small samples at one position), a distribution adds false precision. The adjustment depends on the assumed market risk preference, which is a stated assumption, not a measurement.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the protected and unprotected versions of the same pick (SIn6IyYQEVI [12:46], [15:49]); the numbers are in [[case-study--lakers-2015-pick-protections-removed-about-half-its-value]].

**Related** — [[framework--price-a-protected-draft-pick-like-a-financial-option]]; [[heuristic--market-risk-preference-differs-by-pick-position-in-the-draft-pick-model]].

# Price Risk Differently for Different Pick Positions

**What it is** — In Benjamin Foster's model the Wang transform has one assumption, the market price of risk (gamma), which he reads generally as the market's risk preference (SIn6IyYQEVI [13:17], [13:47], [14:18]). He does not expect pick one to be treated like pick 30. He clusters the player-value distributions by pick (K-means plus a filtering method) into seven asset classes and gives each class its own market price of risk, calibrated on pick-for-pick trades and interpolated where needed (SIn6IyYQEVI [14:18], [14:48]). In his result, pick one stands alone and has a "very risk-seeking" price (teams pay more than expected value), while picks 25 and 30 are "very risk-averse" (teams pay less than expected value) (SIn6IyYQEVI [14:48], [15:19]). He says this matches how trades are talked about: risk and upside at pick one, role players at 25 and 30 (SIn6IyYQEVI [15:19]). He also says the calibration rests on few trades and that more work could be done (SIn6IyYQEVI [14:48]). He names a planned extension: let a team input its own risk preferences, draft-quality expectations or player value metric (SIn6IyYQEVI [19:55], [20:25]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is intuition ("hopefully that aligns with your intuition," SIn6IyYQEVI [15:19]). He gives no tested mechanism.

**When to apply** — As a reminder to state, for each roster spot or acquisition, whether it is bought for ceiling or floor. Inference: a staff could make that an explicit input rather than implicit. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the parameter values are shown on a slide, not read out in the transcript, and are fit to a small number of trades by the speaker's own account (SIn6IyYQEVI [14:48]). Do not carry the pick-one or pick-25 risk values into any other market. The "risk-seeking at one, risk-averse at 25 and 30" statement is an interpretation of calibrated parameters, not a behavioral finding.

**Example** — The speaker's own: pick one's tail, the chance of landing a franchise-changing player, pulls the unprotected price out to the right of its mean, which is why a risk-seeking market pays a premium (SIn6IyYQEVI [13:17], [15:49]).

**Related** — [[framework--price-a-protected-draft-pick-like-a-financial-option]]; [[principle--value-an-uncertain-asset-by-its-outcome-distribution-not-its-mean]].

# Traded Draft-Pick Protections Cluster at Top 5, Top 10 and Top 14

**What it is** — Benjamin Foster shows a figure of picks traded from 2011 to 2017 by level of protection, with three clusters: top-five, top-10 and top-14 protected (SIn6IyYQEVI [05:38]). It is odd, he says, that so many trades need a top-10 protection rather than top nine or top 11, where only one top-11 protection is in the data set (SIn6IyYQEVI [06:08]). The counts are on a slide and are not read out. His hypothesis is that teams cannot easily quantify the difference between top nine, 10 and 11, so they land on round numbers, which the paper calls "psychological anchors" (SIn6IyYQEVI [06:08]). This motivated the research question: could one calculate the value difference between, say, top nine and top 10 (SIn6IyYQEVI [06:39]). He notes protections also raise the chance a trade happens: teams that hold only very high- or very low-value assets can adjust them to assemble a package for a medium-value target in an illiquid barter market (SIn6IyYQEVI [04:37], [05:07]). He says picks 1 to 14 are decided by a lottery (SIn6IyYQEVI [01:32]).

**Why it works** — The anchoring explanation is a hypothesis ("our hypothesis for why this situation might be the case"), not tested (SIn6IyYQEVI [06:08]). The transaction-ease point is the speaker's expectation: protections "appear or ought to" raise the likelihood of a transaction (SIn6IyYQEVI [04:37]).

**When to apply** — As a prompt: where decision rules cluster at round numbers (cutoffs, thresholds, tiers), ask whether the number comes from analysis or from anchoring. Inference: this fits any staff cutoff that sits at 5, 10 or a round percentile. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the pattern is a descriptive figure over seven seasons of one league, the cause is a hypothesis, and the underlying counts are not in the transcript. Round-number clustering could also reflect how many rounds of protection leagues or negotiators find convenient, which the speaker does not rule out. Do not generalize beyond NBA protected picks.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a top-10 protection chosen far more often than top-nine or top-11 (SIn6IyYQEVI [06:08]).

**Related** — [[framework--price-a-protected-draft-pick-like-a-financial-option]].

# A Lottery Based Only on Final Ranking Cannot Favor the Worst Team Without Some Incentive to Tank

**What it is** — Evan Monroe (Stanford PhD student; caption spellings "Monroe" and "Munroe"; joint work with a fellow student the captions call "Martino") says the league's two objectives, backed out from its rule changes and statements, are (1) give the top pick to the lowest-ranked team with as high a probability as possible, subject to (2) removing incentives to tank (-6pe_zOKCig [04:39], [05:09]). Under a lottery that depends only on final win-loss ranking, "it's impossible" to favor the worst team at all without some incentive to tank (-6pe_zOKCig [08:44]). The options are to minimize the incentive by not favoring the worst team, or use a uniform lottery as in 1985 to 1989 (-6pe_zOKCig [08:44]). He quotes a hockey writer's line (caption spelling Greg Wyshynski) that if you do not want tanking you do not want the welfare mechanism that encourages it (-6pe_zOKCig [06:10], [06:41]). History he gives: before 1985 a coin flip between the two conference losers (worst team 50 percent), then an equal lottery for non-playoff teams that cut the worst team's chance to "between 11 and 14 percent" depending on team count (captions garbled), a 1990 figure the captions give as "70%" (looks garbled), 25 percent in 1994, and 14 percent in the most recent change (-6pe_zOKCig [03:09], [03:39], [04:09], [05:39]). He cites prior work showing statistically that teams with incentives to lose late in a season lose more (-6pe_zOKCig [06:41], [07:12]).

**Why it works** — Speaker's argument (intuition, not the proof, which he says is in the paper): once a team is eliminated from the playoffs, its chance of making them is zero, so under a fixed lottery that favors bad teams, losing any game that affects its final ranking improves its draft odds (-6pe_zOKCig [10:49], [11:20]). The league sometimes penalizes egregious cases (-6pe_zOKCig [11:20]). The formal proof is not shown in the talk and was not checked here.

**When to apply** — As a design test for any rule that rewards a poor result: if the reward depends only on the final outcome and favors the weakest, ask whether a rational participant gains by making the outcome worse. Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped after about a year because athletes learned the low-effort answers that looked clean but carried no signal (Explicit, SportSmith, 2026-02-19). Inference: that is a different mechanism (low effort, not deliberate losing) and the link to this result is by analogy only.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the result is a theorem inside a model where teams value only the playoffs and the first pick, at fixed values, and only the first pick is allocated (-6pe_zOKCig [02:39], [09:46]). It covers league policy, not athlete monitoring. Real teams have broader goals, as the speaker says (-6pe_zOKCig [09:46]). His claim that tanking is "most intractable in the NBA" because key players matter so much is an assertion with no data shown (-6pe_zOKCig [02:39]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: an eliminated team late in the season with a lottery that favors bad teams; every game affecting its ranking is one it gains by losing (-6pe_zOKCig [10:49], [11:20]).

**Related** — [[principle--no-tanking-condition-benefit-of-winning-at-least-benefit-of-losing]]; [[framework--time-dependent-lottery-with-dynamically-frozen-odds]].

# The No-Tanking Condition: Winning Must Pay at Least as Much as Losing

**What it is** — In Evan Monroe's model teams care about two prizes, making the playoffs and getting the first pick, each at a fixed value (-6pe_zOKCig [09:46]). A team chooses to try to win or try to lose by a "no tanking condition": the benefit from winning a game must be at least the benefit from losing it (-6pe_zOKCig [10:17]). Winning raises or leaves unchanged the chance of the playoffs, but under the current system lowers the draft chance; losing does the reverse (-6pe_zOKCig [10:17]). The speaker says the condition fails in many scenarios under the current system, with a simple case: a fixed lottery that favors the worst records, applied to a team already eliminated (-6pe_zOKCig [10:49], [11:20]). His design target is that the condition holds in every game (-6pe_zOKCig [21:03]).

**Why it works** — Stated by the speaker as "very intuitive"; the logic is the one-line comparison above (-6pe_zOKCig [10:17]). He gives no further mechanism.

**When to apply** — As a one-question audit of any measure that feeds a consequence: could a participant gain by scoring worse? Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys were abandoned after about a year because the consistent, low-effort answers they rewarded carried no signal, and mRSI from force-plate jumps replaced them as the daily readiness marker as "objective, consistent, and actionable" (Explicit, SportSmith, 2026-02-19). Inference: ask the no-tanking question of each daily number that changes load or playing time (for example, whether a low score lowers practice load, giving an athlete a reason to hold back on a jump). The talk does not claim objective measures are immune, and says nothing about athlete testing; the link is analogy only.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: a model condition, not an empirical finding about teams or athletes. It needs a decision that actually follows from the number and that the participant can see; if the result drives no consequence the athlete cares about, the concern is moot. The two-prize model, rational-actor assumption and fixed prize values are the speaker's simplifications. Do not import the lottery math; a handful of athletes cannot reveal incentives.

**Example** — The speaker's own: an eliminated team facing a fixed, bad-team-favoring lottery should try to lose every game that affects its ranking (-6pe_zOKCig [11:20]).

**Related** — [[claim--lottery-on-final-ranking-alone-cannot-favor-worst-team-without-tank-incentive]]; [[framework--time-dependent-lottery-with-dynamically-frozen-odds]].

# A Draft Lottery That Depends on When Results Happen, With Odds Frozen at a Data-Chosen Point

**What it is** — Evan Monroe says that if the lottery depends on when wins and losses occur, not only on final rankings, it can favor the worst team and remove tanking incentives (-6pe_zOKCig [09:15]). The policy (-6pe_zOKCig [11:55] to [13:26]):
1. After every game, re-estimate each team's probability of finishing last, conditional on results so far; at the start of the season, with equal ability assumed, every team has an equal chance.
2. Set draft odds to match those probabilities, so a long early losing streak raises a team's odds.
3. Freeze the odds at a stopping time chosen dynamically from what happens that season, not a fixed date, since the incentives to win and lose depend on when the streak happens and on who is in the draft.
Early games count more because "uncertainty is actually a good thing" if you are giving a prize to a team that does badly: at the start nobody knows where they will finish, so early losses are a good signal of a bad team and incentives to lose are weak then (-6pe_zOKCig [16:30], [21:03]). The point is to freeze when, in the model, the incentive to win would start to be dominated by the incentive to lose (-6pe_zOKCig [17:00], [17:30]). He says the process removes incentives to tank within a season in the model (-6pe_zOKCig [13:26]). The results he shows come from back-tests: see [[case-study--1989-miami-heat-back-test-of-the-time-dependent-lottery]] and [[claim--rule-degrades-when-the-prize-is-worth-as-much-as-the-playoffs]].

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism: the lottery tracks the posterior chance of finishing last, so the best-supported worst team gets the highest odds, while the freeze point sits where late losing would no longer pay (-6pe_zOKCig [13:26], [17:30]). Proofs are in the paper and not shown.

**When to apply** — As a pattern for any ranking or reward that distorts behavior late: weight early, low-stakes evidence more and stop updating when the incentive to game would dominate. Eric's baseline: no direct link found for rankings; see [[principle--no-tanking-condition-benefit-of-winning-at-least-benefit-of-losing]] for the audit question. Inference: early baseline captures taken before athletes know what a number will change are cleaner reference points, as the applications note suggests.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: back-tests in the speaker's own model, with no real-world trial (the speaker works from a paper in a competition). It depends on a league forecast that accounts for known factors (an injured star returning, trades); if a team knows something the league's forecast does not, gaming remains possible (-6pe_zOKCig [22:03], [22:33], [23:03]). It may increase the incentive to rebuild over several seasons, which the model does not cover (-6pe_zOKCig [13:58], [23:33]). Only the first pick is modeled; the extension to a full draft is in an appendix (-6pe_zOKCig [02:39], [27:10]). The freeze point is stated inconsistently in the captions (see the case study).

**Example** — The speaker's own: the 1989 Miami Heat losing streak at the start of the season (-6pe_zOKCig [16:00], [16:30]).

**Related** — [[claim--lottery-on-final-ranking-alone-cannot-favor-worst-team-without-tank-incentive]]; [[principle--no-tanking-condition-benefit-of-winning-at-least-benefit-of-losing]]; [[claim--model-limits-forecast-gaps-rebuilding-and-single-pick-scope]].

# Case Study: The 1989 Season Back-Test (Miami at 44 Percent)

**What it is** — Evan Monroe back-tests his rule on 1989 because the lottery then was uniform and did not encourage tanking, so his rule's output is, he says, an "unbiased estimate": teams' behavior would have been the same under either (-6pe_zOKCig [14:28], [14:58]). Results: the Miami Heat were the worst team; under the 1989 lottery they had equal odds with other non-playoff teams, but under his rule they get the first pick with 44 percent probability (-6pe_zOKCig [14:58], [15:28]). The Indiana Pacers, who "didn't end up doing all that badly," also get a high probability because their ranking at the freeze point sets the odds and their late winning streak did not count (-6pe_zOKCig [15:28], [16:00]). In his simulation the Heat lose heavily at the start of the season, odds adjust "quite a lot over the first 300 games," and the odds freeze around the 330th game (-6pe_zOKCig [16:30], [17:00]); he also calls this "a third of the way through the season," and the Heat still finished last (-6pe_zOKCig [17:30]). The caption figures (300 games, around the 330th, a third of the season) are slightly inconsistent and are not reconciled here. He says he is "not saying" the Heat tanked; the point is the rule targets the last-place team (-6pe_zOKCig [15:28], [16:00]).

**Why it works** — The speaker explains it as the early losses being a strong signal because early on teams could not yet be gaming (-6pe_zOKCig [16:30]). See [[framework--time-dependent-lottery-with-dynamically-frozen-odds]].

**When to apply** — As an example of choosing a back-test where the baseline behavior is clean: test a new rule on a season whose rules did not distort behavior. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one season chosen by the speaker (he anticipates the cherry-picking objection and shows two harder cases: see [[claim--rule-degrades-when-the-prize-is-worth-as-much-as-the-playoffs]]); a model simulation, not an observed outcome; no ground truth about what teams would have done. The speaker says later seasons are "tainted" because the current rule already changes behavior (-6pe_zOKCig [14:58]). The 44 percent figure depends on the assumed prize values (see the sensitivity entry).

**Example** — The speaker's own, above.

**Related** — [[framework--time-dependent-lottery-with-dynamically-frozen-odds]]; [[claim--2019-season-rule-gives-other-playoff-miss-teams-about-5-percent]].

# The Rule Does Worse When the Prize Is Worth About as Much as the Playoffs

**What it is** — Evan Monroe tries to "break the rule" with a year when a star prospect (named in the captions as Patrick Ewing) is so valuable that the pick is worth about as much as making the playoffs (-6pe_zOKCig [18:01], [18:31]). The rest of the talk assumes the playoffs are worth more than the pick, which lets many games count (-6pe_zOKCig [18:31]). In the stress case the incentives to lose are high, only the first hundred games count, and the Pacers get the pick with the highest probability but only 19 percent, "not as drastic" as the other case (-6pe_zOKCig [18:31], [19:01]). In Q&A, asked how sensitive the model is to the value of the playoffs versus the pick, he says it is very sensitive around one (equal values; going from one to two) and flat once the ratio is three, four or five (-6pe_zOKCig [25:06]). To set it in practice he suggests data work: first-round pick sale values and how a team's fortunes (TV revenue and so on) change with making the playoffs; the rule only needs a lower bound, and if the true ratio is above the number put into the rule, tanking is not encouraged (-6pe_zOKCig [25:37]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reason: when the prize is very valuable, incentives to lose are strong, so the rule can use fewer games and the probability distribution cannot be as skewed (-6pe_zOKCig [18:31], [19:01]). He gives no further analysis in the talk.

**When to apply** — As a check on any incentive-based design: vary the assumed relative value of the two goals and report where results change fast. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one stress case and an oral sensitivity statement, no table or numbers shown beyond 19 percent and the ratio ranges. The bound argument (a lower bound on playoff value is enough) is the speaker's assertion. The stress case is a simulation; the year is only named in captions as a player, so which season it was is not stated in the talk. Do not apply to leagues or sports with different prize structures.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the star-prospect year, where the top team gets 19 percent (-6pe_zOKCig [19:01]).

**Related** — [[framework--time-dependent-lottery-with-dynamically-frozen-odds]]; [[case-study--1989-miami-heat-back-test-of-the-time-dependent-lottery]].

# On the 2019 Season, the Rule Gives the Seven Other Non-Playoff Teams About 5 Percent in Total

**What it is** — Evan Monroe shows the 2019 season under his rule: the second-last team (captions "the feet Suns") gets the highest probability because many of its losses came late in the season, which did not count toward its odds (-6pe_zOKCig [19:31], [20:02]). He compares redistribution: under the current NBA lottery, the other seven non-playoff teams not near the bottom have about 18.5 percent probability of getting the pick, "arguably too high"; under his rule, after 350 games ("not even close to half the season"), the probability that any of those seven ends up last is only 5 percent across all of them (-6pe_zOKCig [20:02], [20:32]). His reading is that the rule "doesn't give the draft to those teams with any like meaningful probability" (-6pe_zOKCig [20:32]). He says the paper includes simulations comparing the rule to the current and uniform rules and finds it performs well (-6pe_zOKCig [21:33]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reason is that odds follow the conditional probability of finishing last, so teams well above the bottom get little (-6pe_zOKCig [13:26], [20:32]).

**When to apply** — As a model of how to report a redistribution result: state the probability mass given to teams who are not the target, current versus proposed. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: simulated, not observed. The speaker warns that 2019 final rankings might have differed under his rule because the current rule encourages tanking (-6pe_zOKCig [19:31]); that is why he calls recent seasons tainted (-6pe_zOKCig [14:58]). The 18.5 and 5 percent figures are single-season outputs and not an average across seasons. The second-last team's high probability illustrates a cost: late losses are ignored by design.

**Example** — The speaker's own, above.

**Related** — [[case-study--1989-miami-heat-back-test-of-the-time-dependent-lottery]]; [[framework--time-dependent-lottery-with-dynamically-frozen-odds]].

# Limits the Speaker Concedes: Forecast Gaps, Multi-Season Rebuilding and Single-Pick Scope

**What it is** — In Q&A Evan Monroe gives four limits on the policy.
1. **Forecast quality.** Asked what happens if an early slump has another cause (a star missing half the season, then returning, or a trade), he says the policy relies on simulating the rest of the season well, as betting markets and draft simulators already do; known factors should go in. If something random happens and the team knows it and the league does not, "there could still be some opportunity to game" (-6pe_zOKCig [22:03], [22:33]). He suggests averaging forecasts from several sites or using an open forecasting tool (-6pe_zOKCig [22:33], [23:03]).
2. **Rebuilding.** A questioner worried that teams with no title hope might lose early and rebuild; he agrees this goes to the rebuilding strategy and the policy may increase that incentive (-6pe_zOKCig [13:58], [23:33]). One response: compute the optimal rule for past seasons, freeze the average, and quantify how much incentive that creates (-6pe_zOKCig [24:04]).
3. **Goal of the draft.** A questioner argued the draft's aim is to redistribute talent, not to reward the worst team, so a policy could produce more badly built teams; the speaker addressed the sensitivity issue rather than this point (-6pe_zOKCig [24:35], [25:06]).
4. **Multiple strong prospects.** The model extends to a sequential lottery by adding terms to the benefit from losing; an appendix in the paper covers it (-6pe_zOKCig [26:40], [27:10]).

**Why it works** — Not a mechanism claim; these are the speaker's own acknowledgements.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when presenting any incentive design: forecast error, multi-period gaming, the goal the rule serves, and scope. Inference: the same four questions apply to a threshold that triggers a load or playing-time change. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the answers are conversational, with no data. The rebuilding suggestion (freeze the historical average) is an idea, not a result shown. Treat these as the speaker's open items, not solved problems.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a star returning mid-season would distort an early record unless the forecast includes the known return (-6pe_zOKCig [22:03], [22:33]).

**Related** — [[framework--time-dependent-lottery-with-dynamically-frozen-odds]]; [[claim--rule-degrades-when-the-prize-is-worth-as-much-as-the-playoffs]].

# Limits the Speaker Concedes: Forecast Gaps, Multi-Season Rebuilding and Single-Pick Scope

**What it is** — In Q&A Evan Monroe gives four limits on the policy.
1. **Forecast quality.** Asked what happens if an early slump has another cause (a star missing half the season, then returning, or a trade), he says the policy relies on simulating the rest of the season well, as betting markets and draft simulators already do; known factors should go in. If something random happens and the team knows it and the league does not, "there could still be some opportunity to game" (-6pe_zOKCig [22:03], [22:33]). He suggests averaging forecasts from several sites or using an open forecasting tool (-6pe_zOKCig [22:33], [23:03]).
2. **Rebuilding.** A questioner worried that teams with no title hope might lose early and rebuild; he agrees this goes to the rebuilding strategy and the policy may increase that incentive (-6pe_zOKCig [13:58], [23:33]). One response: compute the optimal rule for past seasons, freeze the average, and quantify how much incentive that creates (-6pe_zOKCig [24:04]).
3. **Goal of the draft.** A questioner argued the draft's aim is to redistribute talent, not to reward the worst team, so a policy could produce more badly built teams; the speaker addressed the sensitivity issue rather than this point (-6pe_zOKCig [24:35], [25:06]).
4. **Multiple strong prospects.** The model extends to a sequential lottery by adding terms to the benefit from losing; an appendix in the paper covers it (-6pe_zOKCig [26:40], [27:10]).

**Why it works** — Not a mechanism claim; these are the speaker's own acknowledgements.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when presenting any incentive design: forecast error, multi-period gaming, the goal the rule serves, and scope. Inference: the same four questions apply to a threshold that triggers a load or playing-time change. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the answers are conversational, with no data. The rebuilding suggestion (freeze the historical average) is an idea, not a result shown. Treat these as the speaker's open items, not solved problems.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a star returning mid-season would distort an early record unless the forecast includes the known return (-6pe_zOKCig [22:03], [22:33]).

**Related** — [[framework--time-dependent-lottery-with-dynamically-frozen-odds]]; [[claim--rule-degrades-when-the-prize-is-worth-as-much-as-the-playoffs]].
